feedback: If a count is reported while the beam is still moving, prompt: wait for the beam to settle, then read. If it settles tipped to one side, it is not balanced, so add or remove a cube; if no whole number of cubes levels it exactly, record 'about' or 'between' two counts.
If cubes of mixed sizes were used, point out that the count only means something when every unit is identical; redo with one size.
If the estimate was far off, that is fine — the point is to compare your estimate with the measured count and notice the gap.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass can be quantified as a number of identical units that balance the object; the record is a number plus a unit, not just a number.
learnerActions: Place a book (or other object) on one pan of a balance.

Add identical unit-weights (e.g. interlocking cubes) one at a time to the other pan until the beam levels, or is as near level as you can get; if one more cube tips it the other way, the object is between two counts.

Wait for the beam to settle before reading, then count the cubes and record the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes', or 'about 8 cubes' / 'between 8 and 9 cubes' if it never quite levels.
Before you start adding cubes, check every cube is the same size; set aside any odd-sized ones.
Before adding any cubes, estimate how many you expect; after measuring, compare your estimate with the measured count.
activities.title: Balance it with identical units

feedback: If the child says the smaller big-cube count means the book is now lighter or has changed, show one big cube balancing several small cubes, so one big = many small; then the smaller count for the same book makes sense.
If the child claims 15 small cubes is heavier than 10 big cubes just because 15 > 10, compare the actual units directly on the balance: you cannot compare counts made with different-sized units.
Correct reasoning to reinforce: 'bigger cubes are heavier, so fewer of them balance the same book'.
activities.intendedInsight: A larger unit means fewer units are needed to balance the same object; the count changes because the unit changed, not because the mass changed. Conversely, smaller units give a larger count.
learnerActions: Measure the SAME book again, this time using larger unit-weights.
Count how many large units balance the book and compare with the earlier count of small units.
Say aloud why the number is different even though the book has not changed.
Discuss: can both counts be right at the same time — for example '5 big cubes' and '12 small cubes' for the same book? Explain how.
Place one large unit on one pan and add small units on the other until it balances, or is as close as possible — count about how many small units equal one large unit.
Answer: if you used really tiny units instead, would the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
activities.title: Same book, different unit size

feedback: If the child tries to compare counts taken with different-sized units, remind them comparisons only work when the units match.
If ordering is reversed, line up the recorded numbers and check which is larger, then match the symbol.
Encourage a spoken reason for each comparison, not just the symbol.
activities.intendedInsight: Once masses are quantified in the same unit, objects can be compared and ordered numerically and recorded with comparison symbols.
learnerActions: Weigh or read several objects and record each mass with its unit.
Decide which is heavier and which is lighter, and put the objects in order by mass.
Record comparisons using the symbols >, < and = (e.g. 300 g > 200 g).
Explain a comparison aloud, e.g. 'the red bag is heavier because 300 g is more than 200 g'.
activities.title: Compare and order masses from readings
